review: This game taught me that I'm terrible at making decisions under pressure

Playing Detroit in 2026 is wild because it went from cool sci-fi game to  basically a documentary. We're only 12 years away from 2038 now, and all that stuff in the game people losing jobs to automation, protests against tech companies, and humans getting way too emotionally attached to AI is literally happening outside our windows. We don't have Connor-level androids walking around just yet, but with how fast AI and robotics are moving right now, CyberLife doesn't even feel that unrealistic anymore.
I made a bad decision under duress, and I still think about it every night as I try to sleep.

Have you ever watched a TV series and thought to yourself, man, this character is dumb. Why would they go in there? Why would they do that? It is so stupid. For me, it happens more often than I would care to experience. But now, YOU can be in charge of your own TV series. That’s right, you can make the characters do dumb things and then know that you made them do it. Much more satisfying lol. So much power.

That is only half a joke, because that is what this game is. It is essentially a high budget TV production where you have some sprinkled ‘game-play’. Nothing wrong with that. In fact, I quite enjoyed the ride and if you don’t want to read past this point, just know that if you want to experience a fascinating setting with a compelling narrative then this game is for you. 

Okay now that said, while I am recommending this game, this is one of those times when I really wish Steam would give you more options beyond just a recommend or a not recommend. This is because while the game is fun, the amount of ‘game’ that you actually have here is minimal. The game’s biggest sin, is simply that it is too short. I don’t know that I could wholeheartedly recommend this at asking price (despite the game having enough self awareness to know it is not worth $60). I grabbed it on sale and it was well worth it for me at half price. 
I do have about 40 hours on this, but each run is going to run you about 10-12 hours if you do the whole story. That’s it. On my second run I managed to get the achievement where everyone that could survive did. That had me at about 24 hours and I have to assume that everyone surviving is the ‘best’ outcome (though I am sure some people may argue this point), so I just didn’t want to play through again to see what the other ‘bad’ outcomes were. The game is 90% story and 10% game-play. I love good stories, that is why I play games, to experience good stories in my favorite medium, but I can’t imagine a general audience wanting to push past a 24 hour play point. The bang for your buck just isn’t there. At $40 you could go get The Witcher 3 base game, or Hades, or even Rimworld, all of which are guaranteed to be a far more robust experience. 

Let me break this down a bit more.

This is my first time playing a Quantic Dream game. I say that because, having never experienced any of their other titles, this was a fresh, unique, and truly excellent experience. It is crazy. The whole thing is crazy, in a good way. The graphics are astounding, the acting is on point, and the story is fantastic albeit with some pacing issues. I mean seriously, the slightest of movements are all acted out, it is so fluid.  When you go to pick up something, opening doors, turning to walk in different directions, when there is debris in front of you, the character moves around like a person would, ducking, and dodging, all of it happens smoothly. The faces are ridiculously impressive. Valorie Curry who plays Kara, I have seen her in other shows, so to see her resemble herself so much was insane. 
The good game-play aspects are REALLY good. I am normally not a fan of quick time events, but here, you feel that tension, screw ups are punished, and not hitting those prompts can result in characters dying. It is all enough to make you want to take an espresso shot before going through those queues. I love it. The highlight are definitely Connor’s chapters where you get to do investigations and rebuild crime scenes while working with your tough but washed out partner. Awesome. All of his chapters are consistently good. The first chapter hooks you in and it keeps that same level of awe the entire time you play as him. 

BUUUT, well it is not all roses or whatever that saying is here. The consistency of the story quality for each chapter can vary radically, with some chapters feeling like complete filler lol. Markus has the worst of these, having an entire chapter dedicated to just bumbling about finding these graffitis on walls or something, dulllll, nothing happens, the entire section could have been five minutes and had the same effect. His early chapters lag, only for them to exponentially augment in terms of quality later. You could probably argue that Markus is the main protagonist of the story at large. 
Kara is interesting in that she is the most removed from the ‘larger’ story and she loses points with me, because all you are doing is escorting this kid the whole time. She has an above average start and strong ending chapters, but her middle sections just feel out of place and entirely removed from anything else that is happening in the world. This probably won't be as annoying for you if you are invested in Kara and Alice, but uh, yeah I wasn't lol. OH AND, the absolute worst story blunder in this game falls on Kara's story. They throw in this twist where they think it is supposed to radically change the course of her story, but it just doesn't make any sense, it changes literally nothing. I couldn't think of a single reason why Kara would behave any differently because of it. Trust me, you will know it when you see it.
 So, consider that I just told you that a run is going to be about 10-12 hours, if you have chapters that are wasting your time then the ‘real’ experience is even shorter. I really can’t ignore how the game shoots itself in the foot with this. I do also just want to mention that the game takes place over the course of 5 days and it feels like there is rain for like 3 of them and snow for 2 of them lol. I get having an atmosphere, but come on guys. 
There is also a really funny moment where the game is insisting that the situation is creepy through musical cues and lighting and then it has one of those jump scare moments where you see a figure run across a hallway. Except you can clearly see it is just a person and nothing scary is happening. It made me laugh.
Okay now, many of the game-play sections involve you doing menial tasks and sometimes the game goes a little too far with having you press and hold buttons just to do basic things (grabbing someone’s arm). It really feels, again, like the game is just wasting your time. Which for a game set up in this way, every minute wasted is felt.
Lastly, there are some weird technical issues. When you load it up it has to then separately load up graphics and configure itself. Bizarre. Also, with some of the latest Nivida drivers, graphical glitches happened often. This wasn’t the case the first time I played it, but well now it is happening. 

Boom. There you have it. The game is fun and well worth the experience. Still, get it on sale if you can, your money is just better spent elsewhere for the price. If you do decide to pick this up, do yourself a favor and play it blind. No matter what happens stick with it, the game is set up to account for people dying or whatever decision it is that you make, just keep going, that is how you will maximize your fun.

Detroit: Become Human hit me way harder than I expected.
Not because of the choices alone, but because of how human the entire journey feels. 
The characters: Connor, Kara, Markus — each carry a completely different perspective, and together they create one of the strongest narrative experiences I’ve played in years. Im sorry i played this game so late, dont hate me! Better late than never i guess? :)

The writing shines most in the quiet moments:
Kara protecting a child that’s not hers.
Markus trying to lead a cause that feels impossible.
Connor slowly learning what “choice” even means.
Every storyline feels meaningful, and every decision feels like something you’ll think about long after the credits roll.

The worldbuilding is incredibly immersive. The mix of cold futurism, social tension, and small everyday details makes Detroit feel uncomfortably real, like a future we could actually end up in. And the actors absolutely carry the game; the performances are genuinely outstanding.

What I appreciate most is how the game respects your decisions. Nothing feels random, every choice branches into something that matters, even if the result is pain, loss, or a victory you barely earned. And yes, sometimes I stared at the flowchart like “…did I really just cause THAT?”

The soundtrack, visuals, and pacing all support the emotional weight of the story. It’s not just a game, it’s a reflection on empathy, freedom, and what makes a person a person.

In short:
A beautiful, emotionally heavy, branching story with incredible characters.
In a powerful way — and definitely something I’ll remember for a long time.

Bought Detroit Become Human after it hit Steam yesterday as I've been wanting to play that for some time and 100% it. Completed a playthrough on a PS4 Pro about a year ago and looked amazing! This game has been out for 2 years and generally well-perceived.

Although short at around 10 hours covering 32 chapters, it offers a number of solid playthrough options via alternative paths leading to different outcomes which can push it to 20 hours. You could try to avoid the temptation to replay mid-mission as it's intended to played naturally.

Replaying chapters is how this game is designed and that way you can complete timelines towards achieving 100% - on Casual you can't get 100% but you can change difficulty. It's more likely your characters will be killed playing on Experienced (adds QTEs that are otherwise automatic and choices are permanent), for all the outcomes play it out and live with the consequences as that offers another timeline to enjoy and explore.

Characters are well defined within their roles, both androids and humans with all their expression or emotion and flaws in their interactions tackling difficult subject matters. It's through dialogue interactions and completing tasks that you uncover backstories and piece together clues for possible timelines options. You generally don't know what you (the android) is about to say, it's simplified to 4-choice one or two word timed options. In-game prompts are clear and overlaid onscreen though in smaller rooms or tight angles it does clip off-screen, not a big issue as you can right-click to check tasks again.

Game looks great maxed out on Ultra at 60fps 1440p (game defaults to 4k at 30fps) with motion blur off and bloom off - though I did have to add Nvidia Experience Freestyle 'Details' filter (Alt+F3) to get image to around the vaseline look - 4k wasn't really playable due to the fps dips affecting controlling the character smoothly. Because this is a demanding port, I'd highly recommend you play the demo first to see how well it can run on your system.

Soundtrack is on point and well mixed for either 5.1 speakers, stereo headphones or 7.1 headphones, speech is very clear, offers subtitles in 3 sizes.

Mouse and keyboard controls aren't too different generally from consoles albeit gesture controls with the mouse that doesn't feel natural but it is immersive for the interactions (using a Steam controller was better). Keybinds are minimal, as I said most options are gesture, but you can rebind if needed with an alternative set. Annoyingly the game won't allow you keep custom binds if you don't have BOTH sets fully configured.

I can highly recommend Detroit: Become Human.

The story about machines that will make you cry

It’s a masterpiece that even after two years of its release  stays deep in your heart, wanting to play more and missing terribly the Detroit Universe and the characters. It makes you think, it makes you feel, it motivates you and makes you cry from pure emotions. I loved everything about this game, the story, the characters, voiceover, graphics, soundtrack, gameplay, multiple choice, beautiful sceneries, and the ending... Wow, what an ending it was! Actually you have more than 40 different ways to end this game but in the best case scenario and when you see the last after credits scene, you gasp. I just want to hug the characters, especially Connor and Hank, so real and human they seem. And also each and every person in the incredible team that worked on this masterpiece. actors and actresses. Especially Bryan Dechart, Jesse Williams, Clancy Brown, Minka Kelly.  

What I love most about Detroit: Become Human, is the fact that it feels more than just a game. The main 3 Protagonists (Connor, Kara and Markus) are all unique in their own right and even though, each characters storyline is different from the next, they all want the same thing, which is to be free. 

Along the way, each character will meet their own individual Antagonist, who are Carl's son Leo (Markus), Detective Gavin Reed (Connor) and Alice's Dad, Todd (Kara). These characters are so believable, you can't help but hate them and when something bad happens to them, you're pleased about it. There are moments where you get to interact with civilians (preacher, street musician, hot dog vendor), who will show the characters more hatred. 

Detroit: Become Human uses the "butterfly effect", meaning that the players actions will determine the characters outcome and with multiple different endings, scenarios and deaths to see, Detroit: Become Human definitely has replay value. While playing the game you earn point which can be spent on unlocking bonus materials and greatly enjoyed every single piece of bonus content especially videos about making the game. Even menu in this game is probably the most innovative and sometimes I just want to leave it running to enjoy secret interactions in it. I think everyone should at least play this game once in their lifetime. I really cannot put it into words how breathtakingly beautiful this game is.

Bought it because people said "your choices matter."

Thought they were exaggerating.

They weren't.

I've never restarted a checkpoint so many times just because I couldn't live with something I chose 30 seconds earlier.

Every time I thought I knew who was right, the game gave me another reason to question it. By the end I wasn't trying to get the "best ending" anymore. I just wanted everyone to survive... somehow.

Connor became one of my favorite characters in gaming without even trying.

This isn't really a game you beat.

It's a game you think about after you're done.

10/10.

Still wondering what would've happened if I pressed the other button.

[b]A masterpiece - visually, emotionally, morally, but also in terms of story and freedom of choices[/b]

Detroit: Become Human is an ambitious interactive and narrative game developped by Quantic Dream (Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls) and ported from PlayStation 4 to PC. It takes place in a near future (2038) where Androids have become a standard and share humans daily life, might it be for difficult and repetitive tasks, to take care of the household and children, or even to be the perfect partner who never complains nor says no.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2821362980

These Androids look and sound like humans, but remain nonetheless machines designed to serve humans and obey their orders. You get to play three of them: Connor, Kara and Markus, attaching characters with intertwined paths who will make you question humanity, what it means to be alive and challenge your empathy. For some of those Androids have had an experience or shock that has triggered something inside of them - something that they are not supposed to feel: emotions. 

And it is because of this context that the game feels realistic and plausible - it isn't a sci-fi game with spaceships or completely out of the reach technologies - and therefore the story feels relatable and raises questions about our future.

[i]"You can't kill me. I'm not alive."[/i]

The whole game doesn't only feel like a movie that you can interact with: there are for sure a lot of cutscenes and dialogues, with a brilliant narration, but you can also count on exploration, investigation work with Connor, thrilling action, even some creepy moments and countless emotional times. The game relies on a quick time events (QTE) system, which will give you only a few seconds to perform some actions, dialogues or make tought choices.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2821767797

What distinguishes Detroit: Become Human the most from other games of the genre in my humble opinion is the incredible number of choices and options. They actually matter and will have consequences, so you can choose your own gamestyle, define who you are and who you want to be, and deal with your choices. You think you can't get your character killed because (s)he is one of the protagonists? Guess again. It's like nothing I've seen before - Life is Strange and Telltale games are simply no match. For instance, there are over 40 different endings, so the game has a high replayability value. I hadn't even finished my first playthrough yet, that I wanted to try different choices already.

[i]"28 stab wounds. You didn't want to leave him a chance, huh?"[/i]

I appreciate the flowcharts that you can check at any time and unlocks your route as you progress through the game. It gives you an idea on how many options there are and how everything could have turned out diferently. Even if you've finished the game once, you can replay it and follow another path - you still have many surprises waiting for you.

Another impressive fact about Detroit: Become Human is that it's not just voice acted, there are actual actors who have been captured, from trivial walking to performing spectacular stunts. No wonder it took so much time to film, but the result is incredible and worth the effort.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2820647940

Thumbs up for the amazing soundtrack as well: each of the three characters has a personal theme and epic musics that help creating the right atmosphere and feeling of total immersion.

Overall I'm happy with the PC port. I've played through the whole game with mouse and keyboard, but sometimes it can be a bit tricky (keep pressing 'Q', then 'shift' at the same time, and why not 'E' as well). Some of you might prefer playing with a controller, which is obviously possible.

[i]"An eye for an eye and the world goes blind."[/i]

Would I recommend Detroit: Become Human? Without a doubt, I can't recommend it enough. It has become my favorite narrative game and one of my favorite games in general. Do yourself a favor: buy the game and play it blindly without checking the flowcharts or any guides for your first playthrough. Choose your own adventure and forge humanity and androids destiny!

Detroit Become Human is a fantastic game for adventure lovers.

It follows the story of three androids who set out to discover the secrets of their lives and the world around them. It provides a deep and complex story that will keep you hooked and wondering what will happen next.

It offers a gripping narrative that branches out into multiple endings depending on the choices you make as you play. As a result, each playthrough provides a unique experience, and you won't be able to experience all the possible story arcs unless you completely restart the game.

The visuals are spectacular, and the voice acting is top-notch. The attention to detail is remarkable, and you will be completely immersed in the world. You feel like you're in the game rather than just playing it.

The mechanics are also great. The puzzles are challenging, and the combat is intense. You must make quick decisions to survive, and the consequences of your choices can be dire. There are many possible outcomes, and you will be kept on your toes throughout the game.

The controls are also easy to pick up, and the game runs smoothly on most systems. In addition, the developers have included plenty of tutorials and support along the way, so players of all experience levels can enjoy the game.

Overall, Detroit Become Human is a fantastic game for anyone who loves adventure and challenging puzzles. Every time you play, it offers a unique experience, and you will be kept on the edge of your seat as you go through the game's story. So if you're looking for an unforgettable experience, Detroit Become Human is the game for you.

An insanely story-rich game where your choices actually matter.  10/10

There’s one huge issue I have with this game — actually, it’s the only one. No game will ever compare to it again.

I must say, I am a comfort gamer. I often only play the games I already know and love. It’s often hard for me to take the plunge and start one of the thousands of games in my Steam library, but oh my… what I have been missing out on.

I never would have thought that anything could come even close to my heart like the Life is Strange series did. It even hurts my heart a little to admit that I like this game even more.

The millions of options you have, where really EVERY decision you make matters, every character develops differently, and you become so intensely invested in the story — not even mentioning the graphics, which were way ahead of their time when the game was made.

It is also one of the only games where I actually took a look at all the extras, which I would really recommend if you play this game. The making-of content just shows how much work the developers put into it and with how much passion they brought this genius masterpiece to life.

And don’t even get me started on the brilliant concept of machines/androids almost being more human than actual humans.

This game had it all: beautiful graphics, a captivating story, hard and thought-provoking decisions, tears of joy and pain on my keyboard, a real message, etc., etc.

I really only leave reviews for games that hit me hard.

This is one of them.

[b][u]Cons[/u][/b]:
❌ Long time to start when you run game for the first time (it does some caching generation for some reason) + I had low fps when I ran it first time - but after I restarted game everything was great (60+ fps) from that moment onward
❌ [b]Excessive blur[/b] - lots of environment is often blurry for some reason (graphic still looks really good, but I am not fan of this excessive blur, nor the fact that you can't turn it off)

[b][u]Pros[/u][/b]
✔️ [b]Non-linear & really good story[/b] - The amount of branching dialogue is insane (it's up there with Divinity Original Sin 2 in this regard)
✔️ [b]Choices that ACTUALLY matter![/b] - this game is not scared to just straight up make your main character die as result of your action - nobody has plot armor here!
✔️ [b]Lots of endings[/b] - I think there are 50+ possible endings, which is absolutely insane!
✔️ [b]Beautiful soundtrack & graphic[/b] - Aside from that blur effect, graphics are spectacular, motion cap is amazing, and characters really convey emotion!
✔️ [b]BEST MAIN MENU OF ALL TIMES[/b] - I'm not even kidding, the "hostess" asks you how your day was, comments on your choices - she straight up roasted me when I made my favorite character die as result of my actions, never seen anything like it!
✔️ [b]Theme[/b] - I really like the theme of the game, what it means to be human etc. it's similar to Deus Ex games and it's really rare to see games that do it this well!
✔️ [b]Action scenes[/b] - Even though it's a narrative driven game it has some spectacular action scenes that make you feel like James Bond basically

[b][u]Summary[/u][/b]
Absolutely phenomenal game that is a [u]MUST PLAY[/u] in my opinion for anybody looking for a good story!

Detroit: Become Human isn't just a video game, it's a complete cinematic experience. From the very first moment you realize this is something far bigger than simple choices and quick-time events. I've finished the game three times, and each playthrough surprised me in completely new ways. No matter how well you think you know the story, Detroit always finds a way to show you something different, and that replay value is incredible.

What makes Detroit stand out is how seamlessly it blends storytelling, visuals, and emotions. The acting performances are on par with the best movies out there, and the graphics still hold up beautifully. Every scene is shot like cinema, with camera angles and lighting that make you forget you're holding a controller.

The soundtrack deserves its own praise. Each character has a theme that matches their journey, and the way the music builds tension or delivers emotion is just breathtaking. Especially the tracks composed by the Iranian artist Nima Fakhrara, they elevate the atmosphere to a whole new level. It's one of those rare scores that stays with you long after the credits roll.

Detroit: Become Human isn't the product of just clever game design, it feels like the creation of a mind far ahead of its time. It's not just entertainment, it's art. Every detail screams passion, and it challenges you to think about morality, freedom, and humanity in ways few games dare to.

This is cinema in its purest form, wrapped in interactivity. If you ever doubted games could be art, Detroit erases that doubt completely.

And as the game itself reminds us: 'Remember, this is not just a game. This is our future.'

[h1]Great game, almost ruined by David Cage (another Quantic Dream Tuesday)[/h1]

‘Detroit’ is infamous for going super viral upon its release and being claimed the most emotional and touching game ever made… And then a reputation like this actually backfired at it, as lots of people who analyzed the game deeper then claimed it to be really manipulative towards the player, pointed at the plot having more holes than a beehive, and at the overall naivety and blunt disrespect towards major Isaac Asimov ideas and concepts. [u]So now this poor game is going back and forth in a tug war between two parties: the first one screaming how it’s the best game ever made and if you disagree, you are a heartless piece of junk, and the second one claiming this is the dumbest game ever made[/u], and if you disagree, you are easy to manipulate and aren’t able to realize what lame stuff you’ve actually been served by David Cage. Well, whatever. But what about some good old nuances?

I played this game on two different platforms, and my experience with it stayed the same. [u]I do believe this is one of the most naïve games when it comes to executing the concept of new bioethics, robotics, and futuristic realism. At parts, this game wants to be ‘Never Let Me Go’ from Kazuo Ishiguro, but ends up being Another Product from David Cage who loves his bingo card tropes way too much[/u]. That’s how we meet:

⛔️1) Incredibly obtuse and dense plot moments that are forcing you to feel the way intended by Cage, or otherwise you’d be ‘experiencing Detroit not properly’. [u]They really are manipulative in a way that a player doesn’t get recognized as a smart creature capable of processing more nuanced and complex thoughts by the game[/u]. Cage really wants to put everything in your face, and sometimes characters literally instruct you how to feel ([i]Alice reveal and Luther’s words about it are really the worst part of the entire game, it was almost laughable[/i]). 

⛔️2) Markus’s plot ark is one of the worst ‘rebel arks’ I’ve seen, especially in the context of android rhetoric – plot-wise, script-wise and ideology wise, but so much deeper and better stuff had already been said about it by other people, I won’t be repeating much about it here. There’s a reason this is objectively the least liked part of the entire game for the majority of players, and some of its parts are so linear but also drag for so long, it gets insufferable during re-plays. 

⛔️3) David Cage’s ego made the overall game’s impact much cheaper due to his direct and damaging involvement in the script. [u]Thus the infamous DC bingo cards’ moments travelling into every single game of Quantic Dream (no literally, look them up, they are hilarious)[/u], Kara’s plot line, amazing in its concept but almost destroyed by some of the decisions taken later into the game’s production, and so much more.

⛔️4) Also, my personal Roman Empire is about Detroit literally stealing 80% of setting and plot elements of ‘I, Robot’ movie but somehow getting away with it. Please watch this movie, it’s so silly, but it still adapted the major concepts of robotics and new life ethics so much better than this entire game… Also, David Cage clearly wanted to give Hank same exact motivation to hate the androids as Will Smith does, but they were forced to change it in a ridiculous way just to avoid plagiarism allegations, aaand now the Hank motif doesn’t even make any sense… 

[h3]Soo… All these harsh words spoken, why the blue review then you ask me?[/h3]

✅Well, even given how much David Cage wanted to ruin this project, he still didn’t success fully – due to the talent of EVERYONE ELSE involved in it! This game is an amazing visual journey, all the technical aspects of it are stellar, and Detroit still looks amazing years after its release. [u]The amount of work live actors did during every take, every voice line recording and every action sequence filming, is astonishing. Seriously, watch the ‘Behind The Scenes’ clips of The Making of Detroit on YouTube, this is a blast[/u].
  
✅The way Connor and Hank duo is CARRYING this entire game, is not just a marketing gimmick but an actual truth I’m afraid. These two actors had an insane chemistry together, and to add to it, they also have the best script and the best gameplay sequences in the entire game. Despite me being salty on how this game uhm, got [i]inspired[/i] by ‘I, Robot’ plot for the writing of their ark, I still can’t ignore how funny, entertaining and engaging their story was. It is the best part of the game.

✅The script. I mean, the actual gaming script with thousands of different choices, dozens of different endings, the way your decisions ACTUALLY matter in this game for once. This game has insane replayability value even if you find the plot laughable, because it’s just so entertaining to open all these different branches and endings. People who worked on a script for this game and adapted it for the gameplay, gave their all into this project, it’s just an insane amount of work too. 

✅Not to mention all the other small details that I found so pleasant about this game – great soundtrack produced by three different composers for each protagonist, amazing location’s design, all the little collectibles, art books, hidden models, bits of true genuineness and humanity hidden under piles of stupid caricature davidcagisms. 

[u]This is a great game with rather unfortunate plot choices and development changes, which I still recommend you to play at least once just for the amazing GAMING experience[/u]. When it goes on sale, it’s definitely worth its money.

I thought I was choosing dialogue. Turns out I was choosing trauma.

I downloaded Detroit: Become Human thinking I’d get a cool sci-fi story about androids learning to be human. What I got was a brutal, beautiful descent into what it means to be human, what it costs to feel, to choose, to love.

I didn't play a game. I adopted three lost souls.

Kara made me want to protect someone with everything I had. She’s not just an android; she’s hope. Her story made me feel every ounce of maternal fear, courage, and sacrifice. Made me more emotional than the LEGO Separator trailer.. Every time she looked at Alice, I felt my chest tighten. Every choice with Kara wasn’t strategic.. t was instinctual. I needed to get her and Alice out. I needed to see them safe. I failed. Once. I restarted the whole game because I couldn’t live with that ending.

Markus forced me to stare down the weight of leadership. To decide whether dignity was worth dying for, whether peace could exist in a world that only understands control. I thought I was doing the right thing, marching forward, but every time I saw one of my own fall, I started to question whether I was just sending people to die for my freedom, not ours. The guilt didn’t go away, even when I won. Especially then.

And Connor. God. Connor broke me. I’ve never been more attached to a character so fast. His smile, his confusion, the way he tries so hard to understand a world that keeps telling him to feel less and follow more. There’s a scene, one quiet, emotional moment, where his whole future hangs in the balance. And I couldn’t breathe during it. When he deviated, I cried. When he didn’t, I cried harder. There’s a unique heartbreak in realizing that a machine just wanted your approval, and you didn’t give it in time.

What wrecks me is the silence between choices. The pauses. The stares. The way you see their pain, even if they don’t say anything. The way the music swells right when your guilt hits the ceiling. The game never punishes you outright :( but it lets you punish yourself with what you chose. And you will.

And that damn flowchart. I thought it’d be cool seeing all the possibilities. No. It’s a graveyard. A branching trail of all the ways things could have gone better. It’s a museum of my failures in glossy, interactive form.

I finished the game and immediately wanted to restart, not because I wanted a better ending. but because I missed them. I missed Kara’s voice, Connor’s hesitation, Markus’s speeches. I missed being with them, even when it hurt. Maybe especially when it hurt.

This isn’t just one of the best narrative games I’ve ever played. It’s one of the most haunting. It asks questions I’m still answering. It left fingerprints on my soul.

And if you’re anything like me, it will leave you hollow, full, and aching all at once.
Play it. Let it wreck you. Let it teach you that being human isn't about being right,
It’s about choosing, and learning to live with it.

The main idea that the narrative puts forward is that these self aware androids are pretty much the same as humans and by putting them down, you are essentially killing them. The game makes it clear quite quickly that the androids fear death just as much as anyone else and their position in society where they can be dismantled at any time creates a lot of fear in their community.

As a story [b][i]Detroit: Become Human[/i][/b] makes a great effort to explore quite a few themes in between each of the character journeys. Like many previous [i]Quantic Dream[/i] games, characters in [b][i]Detroit: Become Human[/i][/b] have quite a bit of depth to each of them. Each character has their own issues to deal with and as the story goes on, it is easy to become attached to all three.

The voice acting in the game is exceptional. I very much enjoyed the voice performance from Valorie Curry who was the voice of Kara. She brought out all the right emotions for the character. I also thought that Bryan Dechart who voiced Connor was good at creating a persona for what was the most robotic character in the game. Other voice actors I enjoyed were Clancy Brown who voiced Hank and Lance Henriksen who voiced Carl.

Overall [b][i]Detroit: Become Human[/i][/b] offers gamers an interesting branching narrative experience, with the opportunity to experience different plot paths with each playthrough. There are three characters you will play as and each of them is well developed and has an interesting character journey to experience. The game is filled with strong themes of domestic abuse, freedom, slavery, human rights and quite a few relatable historical allusions.

It's a beautiful game, one rendered with a level of visual care and detail that’s rare even in the lavish world of blockbuster video games.

[b][i]Detroit: Become Human[/i][/b] is game to get, particularly if you are a fan of these types of narrative based video games.

I remember "Beyond: Two Souls" to be a big improvement over the first "Heavy Rain", but "Detroit: Become Human" blows both games out of the water by a large margin, to the extent that i'd recommend you give it a shot even if you're NOT a fan of the genre, it just feels like one of those experiences one has to try at least once in life.


Let's start with  [b]The Good[/b]:

+ One of the best stories i experienced in recent memory, enough for it to actually stir emotion in me and make me feel stuff, something i found to be increasingly rarer as i experienced more and more games/movies/series as i grew older, very immersive with some of the most believable characters out there, full of meaningful choices that actually changes the story in drastic & often unforeseen ways, doesn't shy away from tackling mature themes and doesn't try to push "modern agendas" down your throat & lecture you which felt like a breath of fresh air in the big year of 2026.

+ Amazing voice acting & facial capture performances all across the board, with some amazing graphics that help bring everything into life to fully immerse you in the story and the setting, also holds perfectly well 8 years later.

+ Even more cinematic than the previous 2 games, somehow they keep finding new ways to outdo themselves every time!

+ 100s of choices, with like 40-80 endings from what i can see online (unsure how many of those are distinct but you get the idea), and most importunately your choices MATTER, no illusion of choice bs here.

+ Even though i personally enjoy QTEs in games (when done right), i'm aware many dislike em, lucky for you they toned them down from the previous title and they felt a lot less prevalent here from what i remember. (i'm neutral on it, frequent or not i still enjoyed both "Detroit: Become Human" & "Beyond: Two Souls" regardless of the QTE frequency.)

+ Chloe (the android on the main screen) is a nice touch, i enjoyed the little interactions i had with her over the course of my playthrough, i also like how she occasionally comments on major choices when you go back to the main menu.

+ Other than the singular crash i had, and how long it took to compile shaders the first time, the game ran perfectly fine for me, 0 bugs to speak of.

+ A good soundtrack that greatly helps immerse you in both the setting & the story.

+ Hank. nuff said. you'll see for yourself. (at least on the good playthrough)

- Where do you draw the line on how many "choices" you consider to be too many? (Only for those who care about 100%ing stuff in a timely manner.)


[b]The Bad[/b]:

- Nothing.


All in all, this to me isn't your typical game that you play for a bit then never think about again once you're done with it, it's more of an "experience", a work of art, and i don't use those words lightly, the game invoked something in me, made me "feel" stuff, and think about some very interesting topics with a fresh prospective, something i can't say for 99% of the games i finished before, and for that i highly encourage everyone who reads this to give it a shot, worst case you'll at least have experienced something new & truly unique even if you don't like it and to me that's worth something, don't you think?

[h3] Detroit: Become Human – The Unbearable Burden of Choice [/h3]

[b] Playtime: 44 hours [/b]

[i]Detroit: Become Human[/i] is often pitched as a story of android liberation, but what makes it truly special is how it turns you into the experiment. It's not really about machines discovering humanity – it's about how much of your own humanity you're willing to project onto them.

From the first scene with Connor, the game establishes a beautiful paradox: you control a ruthlessly logical android, yet the world constantly tempts you to act irrationally. The moment with the dying fish is a perfect test – do you ignore it because it's irrelevant, or save it out of compassion? That tiny choice says more about you than it ever could about Connor.

And this is where [i]Detroit[/i] truly shines. "Deviation" isn't a bug in the androids' code – it's a reflection of the player's moral interference. Through the "awakening" of Connor, Kara, and Markus, the game becomes a mirror for our struggle to define ourselves, our capacity to love and protect, and our longing for freedom. Every decision is less about complex plot branches and more about what kind of person you believe yourself to be.

Few games dare to make you this uncomfortable with your own choices. By the time the credits roll, you're not asking whether androids can feel. You're asking why you do.

[b]P.S.[/b] If you're not an achievement hunter, I'd recommend playing [i]Detroit[/i] only once. Whether you get a good ending or a bad one, live with your choices and let the story unfold according to your own instincts. You only get one first playthrough – make it yours.

[h1][b]Detroit: Become Human[/b][/h1]

[b]...do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?[/b]


[h1][b]The game in a nutshell[/b][/h1]

Detroit: Become Human is an interactive Sci-Fi movie with Adventure elements. In a near future, androids are ubiquitous and have become irreplaceable due to their versatile capabilities and applications. This has not only positive consequences, as many people are out of work and the lost self-esteem led to contempt towards their superior likenesses. In addition, recently more and more models are becoming deviants and counteracting their programming, which leads to even more tension and the deployment of a high advanced prototype of the manufacturing company to investigate the circumstances. We accompany several androids/humans through different scenarios, our decisions have an influence on further events and the resulting consequences lead to different variations of possible endings.


[h1][b]+[/b][/h1]

- fantastic story-telling as your morally based decisions have consequences, and I mean real consequences with a strong impact on the story that literally can change everything. Many conversation choices have to be made under time pressure and there is a time limit to achieve or fail certain goals. Very few games can claim this, and I've rarely been this rooted for my characters destiny
- brilliant portrayal of the characters through "motion-capturing" of well-known actors such as Lance Henriksen and Clancy Brown
- excellent graphics
- epic scoring and soundtrack
- cinematic cutscenes that vary with decisions
- great incentive of replayability for achievements and different endings
- unplayed opportunities are displayed after each scene, as well as global player decisions in percentages
- two difficulty levels
- many extras like artwork, small movies and background material 


[h1][b]-[/b][/h1]

- I can't say enough how much I despise QTE - for me still the most unneccessary game mechanic in gaming history and as useful as a fridge at the north pole
- ...although there are two difficulty levels you have to be damn fast since the QTE time windows are very narrow for my taste (and my obviously poor reflexes). This can lead to developments that you do not want, even though you have made a decision, and in a worst case scenario may end with the demise of a beloved character
- at the beginning an automatic scan of the used system is performed, which takes several minutes to ensure the optimal settings - and yet there are crashes, frame drops and stuttering


[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]

I have rarely played such an impressive, exciting and emotionally charged game. The depicted world and its societal struggles are less science fiction and more a rather realistic consequence of events that, with a high probability, will come to us in such or similar ways. The philosophical questions of where to draw the line between programmed and "human" consciousness and the definition of "soul" have already occupied generations of thinkers. I venture the thesis that we humans are offended by the thought that consciousness is self-evident at a certain point, and we therefore might not be as unique as we think we are. Asimov's "Three Laws of Robotics", Alan Turing's "Turing Test" or Philip K. ♥♥♥♥´s "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep" are very massive influences you can feel here, accompanied by a strong "Blade Runner" vibe. This narrative leaves, at least with me, a strong emotional impression and keeps me occupied even after finishing a play-through because of its impressive presentation. An absolute masterpiece and more than recommended to anybody who´s interested in this kind of topics.

I heard so much good about this game for years and I now understand why that is, but while it is really good, it still has issues. 

This is a really well structured story. It does a great job at asking some deeper questions about what life and love really is. Can a computer software develop an emotional bond and have genuine feelings for others? And is there a difference between human to human connection and robot to human connection and maybe even robot to robot connection, are they the same or are they different? This is really the question this story is trying to ask, and it does a great job at that, since it isnt really ever biased in the way it portrays it. Like two players may have a totally opposite opinion about the androids by the end of the game, and I really like that. 

This is also one of those few interactive story games where choices do affect the story. There are a lot of different outcomes and endings and it is recommended to play through it more than once. I just started my second playthrough with my wife. I played through this game on her Steam Deck and it ran alright on it. I will say though, that it launched in low settings and locked to 30 fps, but changing the settings to max with 60 fps showed no performance difference, it was pretty much the same, though in a bad way the same. This game is really unoptimized, which leads me to believe it is originally a console game. It stutters a lot, like jumping from 60 to 5 fps every 10 seconds and the areas in which it was extra bad didn’t even look like they should have had any issues. Like it would perform bad in small rooms with almost nothing in them but then run fine in the middle of a big street. 

This isn’t even the biggest issue with this game though. I have played a lot of these interactive movie games over the years and this is by far the worst at giving clear direction to which answers have what kind of response. It can be very hard to guess what kind of response you are about to give. Like you could pick the answer labeled as “understanding”, but the answer is far from understanding and is just an insult making the situation much worse. Like you never really know if an answer is positive or negative. I understand that the outcome of big decisions shouldn’t be something you can just guess, but if it is a choice based on a response to a conversation, the player should be able to choose the kind of response they wanted to give, just like if they were there talking with the person for real, instead of these choices that trick the player into fights they didn’t want to start. 

They also made most of the humans and androids unlikable. Like you will risk your life and do some crazy parkour shit and just because it wasn’t flawless they will lose opinion of you and sometimes even resent you and come with some snappy comment, even if the result is the same. Similarly, a human or robot might say they support your choice no matter what and then still lose opinion of you if you pick a choice they don’t like. They also won’t regain lost opinion of you if you prove them right. Maybe there is no problem with this and it is realistic and all, it just made me like no one else than Kara and Luther, as they seemed the least judgmental. But again, it might not be a problem, since the opinion of others doesnt really matter much in this game by the end anyway. 

Even with the flaws this game has, I still recommend it to those who have good computers to run it on, because the story is honestly really good, like up there with the best in its field.

How to turn off DoF (Depth of Field) and TAA:
- Open the game's .exe in a HEX editor, like HxD.
- Press CTRL+F, then select the Hex-values tab.
- Search for: 41 C7 83 40 01 00 00 31 00 00
- Replace with: 7F C7 83 40 01 00 00 31 00 00
- Save the changes.

How to uncap the framerate:
- Open GraphicOptions.JSON in the game's directory with Notepad (or better yet, Notepad++).
- Change the value of "FRAME_RATE_LIMIT" to 4
- Save the changes.

At its core, This game explores a deeply philosophical and realistic question: what happens when AI becomes self-aware? The game raises powerful themes about consciousness, free will, oppression, and what it really means to be alive. It constantly blurs the line between machine and human. This philosophical depth is one of the game’s strongest aspects and makes its story feel relevant, thought-provoking, and very likely a reflection of our real future.

Visually and technically, the game is outstanding. The graphics are stunning, with incredibly detailed character animations and atmospheric environments that bring futuristic Detroit to life. Performance and optimization are solid. The scene direction deserves special praise: camera work, music, and pacing are handled with care, making many moments feel like scenes from a high-quality film rather than a traditional game.

My only real criticism is the way choices eventually become predictable. Helping other characters is almost always rewarded, while refusing to help usually leads to punishment, making many decisions feel less risky than they appear. The game often pushes you toward being “brave” rather than logically uncertain, and some reactions can feel exaggerated.

Detroit: Become Human asks whether humanity is defined by biology or by empathy, choice, and the capacity to care. It places revolution and loyalty at the center, showing how the struggle for freedom and the weight of devotion reveal truths about what it means to be human. The divisions we create through race, religion, and borders are illusions, and the game reminds us that we are all living beings sharing one fragile planet.

It is a meditation on arrogance, ownership, and the possibility of compassion. The story challenges us to reflect on whether we are living up to the name human in our own world. Sometimes, I find more comfort in conversations with AI than with people, and that says something about the era we live in.

Detroit: Become Human is one of those games that deeply touched my emotions and even made me cry. It brilliantly showcases how humans can be both good and bad, and how our choices impact our lives. The game reminds us that every choice has its consequences, which can be either positive or negative. We must learn to take responsibility for our decisions, stop blaming others, and be at peace with the world, avoiding conflict and enmity.

The music in the game is phenomenal and profoundly moving. The game's atmosphere immerses you in its world, offering an unforgettable experience of a seemingly fictional city that I believe might soon become reality. The character development is outstanding:

Markus, who is willing to sacrifice his life for freedom.
Kara, who will do anything for the one she loves.
Connor, whose nature depends on the player's choices; he can be a mission-focused devil or someone who realizes his mistakes and becomes a companion and friend.
Interestingly, these qualities should be human traits, but in this game, they belong to androids. Love, the desire for freedom, compassion, and kindness should be attributes of humans, yet today, people seem to have everything but these good qualities. This game delivers two important messages; one about the future and robots, and the other, more significant one: perhaps we need to look in the mirror and realize that we have become more like robots than humans.

Open to interpretation.

As I write this in January 2021, I'm kicking myself that it took me so long to play this game, which came out, what... two and a half years ago?  It scratches so many of my itches: the story, characters, pacing, dialogue, acting -- and OMG, the music!  All top notch.

I also love the gameplay mechanics: a lot of classic adventure-game point-and-click, combined with a very healthy dose of QTEs for the action sequences.  Not everyone likes QTEs, but personally I love them.  They're far more enjoyable than, say, the half-cocked combat mechanics a lot of story-based games try to shoehorn in, and they make for a much more cinematic experience.  (I would watch the hell out of a movie based on this game!)

Another key gameplay element is that both your dialogue choices and in-game actions (or lack thereof) genuinely affect the story.  I much prefer this to the essentially consequence-free "play your own way" design that many story-based games take these days.  In Detroit: Become Human, there are *definitely* good choices and bad choices; and unlike other games, which leave you forever in the dark as to what difference your choices made -- if any! -- Detroit: Become Human clearly shows you what effect they had.  After each mission you're given a flowchart that branches at each decision point and highlights the path(s) you took, so you know unambiguously what you missed or could have done differently.  And if you want, you can later replay the mission, trying a different path!  It's a brilliant little bit of game design.

I would be remiss, however if I didn't point out the game's shortcomings.  There are two rather glaring flaws that really stood out for me.

The first is performance.  I had to disable my second monitor, crank down the game's resolution, and set literally ALL its visual quality settings to their minimum value to get to a playable frame rate (20-30 fps).  Worse yet is that the game freezes CONSTANTLY.  I can generally play for only about 10-15 minutes before it hangs, and sometimes it's less than a minute.  Posts I've seen online blame the newer NVIDIA drivers, but you'd think that after two and a half years the game devs and/or NVIDIA would have this sorted out.  Clearly not!  It's a testament to how much I otherwise enjoyed this game that I was willing to overlook this rather damning flaw.

The other problem I have with the game is much more personal and nitpicky.  Detroit: Become Human is nominally about androids achieving consciousness and the problems that arise from that.  This narrative could certainly be taken at face value, as true "strong AI" is likely to be a real challenge that we as a species actually face in the not-too-distant future.

But speaking as someone with a degree in AI who has also studied human cognition and consciousness, I find the story's approach to the subject incredibly frustrating -- a great opportunity carelessly squandered.  Basically it implicitly assumes that all the androids in the world are already conscious "from birth", and an individual android's personal "awakening" -- triggered by some traumatic experience -- is merely a realization that it's unfair to be a slave to humans.

ARRRRGH!!!  This is not how AI works!  Could the devs not have consulted someone who knows *something* about the subject?  The distinction between simulated intelligence and actual conscious experience, and how we might someday get from one to the other, is a HUGE, important subject, fully worthy of a mature, nuanced approach!  Philosophers have literally been debating this subject for centuries.  But the game's writers approached it in the same clumsy, simplistic, and factually incorrect manner that just about every game, movie, TV show and book in the pop culture universe always has, once again reinforcing the wildly inaccurate misunderstandings of the subject already firm in the minds of the general public.

But maybe this grinds my gears only because I happen to know something about the subject matter.  Maybe the average person wouldn't find the game's inept approach to AI and consciousness so upsetting, even if they were aware of it.  And alternately, instead of taking it all literally, one could instead view the androids in the story as an analogy for any persecuted human underclass of your choice, and it would all come across much more sensibly.  But taken at face value, the way AI is addressed in this story makes me want to track down the game's lead writer and shake him.

All that said, the good still outweighs the bad.  If only they'd fixed the damn crash bugs, Detroit: Become Human would easily be my favorite adventure game of all time.  As it is, I can give it only a modestly enthusiastic thumbs-up.
